canonical_question: Are the metal oxides/hydroxides formed from HCl reactions considered stable or do they decompose at the test temperatures (450°C/650°C)?

question_variants.question: Are the metal oxides/hydroxides formed from HCl reactions considered stable or do they decompose at the test temperatures (450°C/650°C)?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The provided evidence confirms the formation of metal oxides/hydroxides via HCl reaction with moisture impurity but does not explicitly state their thermal stability or decomposition behavior at 450°C/650°C. It notes the formation of highly corrosive HCl and oxides but leaves the fate of the oxides at these temperatures unaddressed in the supplied spans.

answers.answer: The interaction between chlorides and moisture impurity in the salt results in the formation of highly corrosive HCl and metal oxides/hydroxides. The provided text does not confirm if these oxides decompose at 450°C or 650°C.
answers.measurement_outcome: Formation of HCl and metal oxides/hydroxides observed; decomposition status unreported.
answers.mechanism: Interaction between chlorides and moisture impurity leads to HCl and oxide formation.
answers.boundary_limitation: The evidence spans do not specify the thermal stability or decomposition temperature of the formed metal oxides/hydroxides.
evidence_spans: Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205).
The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205.
Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205.
